title: Westmark inflation (fictional) beats forecasts: a calm market
setup: Fictional Westmark publishes its monthly [[inflation]] figure. The [[central-bank]] targets 2%. Over the past month WMK has moved sideways, and the economic calendar showed no other big release that day. All figures are made up; this is a practice scenario, not a forecast.
pricedIn: Little. Most traders expected the central bank to hold its [[interest-rate]] at the next meeting, and few had bet on a high inflation number. WMK had been flat going into the release.
question: Inflation comes in at 3.4% against a 3.0% consensus, a +0.4-point surprise. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: WMK rises and holds as traders start to expect a rate rise.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: little was priced in, so a higher-than-expected number can shift rate expectations and the currency with them.

reactions.text: WMK rises at first, then gives some back as traders read the rest of the report.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: other parts of a report, such as which prices drove the rise, can soften the first reaction.

reactions.text: WMK hardly moves because a bigger story elsewhere dominates the day.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: a release can be outweighed by other news or by the general mood in markets.

reactions.text: WMK is certain to rise by a fixed amount for every 0.1 points of surprise.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: there is no fixed exchange rate between surprise and price. Reactions vary from day to day.

reactions.text: WMK cannot move until the central bank actually meets.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: prices move on what traders expect the bank to do, long before it meets.

takeaway: With little priced in, a surprise has more room to move the price. But even then, several reactions are plausible. Compare this with the crowded version of the same release.
